lead: Flame velocity is how fast the flame front moves through the chamber. Together with the area of the front and the density of the unburnt charge, it fixes the mass burning rate, the kilograms of charge burnt each second. The mass burning rate, in turn, sets the rate of pressure rise, dp/dθ, in bar per degree of crank angle. That slope decides where peak pressure falls, how much work comes out, how rough the engine sounds and how close it runs to knock.
prereq: You need: the three stages of SI combustion and the p–θ diagram (stages of combustion).

sections.h3: Flame speed, burning velocity and flame velocity

items: Laminar burning velocity SL: the speed of a smooth flame front relative to the unburnt gas just ahead of it, in still gas. For petrol–air at room conditions it is about 0.3 to 0.5 m/s. It is highest for a slightly rich mixture (equivalence ratio φ ≈ 1.1, where φ is the actual fuel–air ratio divided by the chemically correct one) and rises with the unburnt gas temperature.

Turbulent burning velocity ST: the same idea in turbulent gas. Eddies wrinkle the front, so more fresh charge meets the reaction zone each second. A simple estimate is ST ≈ SL + u′, where u′ is the turbulence intensity (the r.m.s. fluctuation of gas velocity). In an engine u′ is about half the mean piston speed, a few m/s, so ST is a few m/s.

Flame travel velocity (often just "flame velocity" or "flame speed" in textbooks): the distance the front moves across the chamber divided by the time, measured relative to the cylinder head. It is larger again, of the order of 15 to 40 m/s, because the expanding burnt gas pushes the front outward on top of its burning velocity.

blocks.text: So a 40 mm flame path burnt in 1.4 ms gives a flame travel velocity of 0.040 ÷ 0.0014 ≈ 29 m/s, even though the front burns into the charge at only a few m/s.

sections.h3: Flame front area and the mass burning rate

blocks.text: ṁ<sub>b</sub> is the mass burning rate (kg/s); ρ<sub>u</sub> is the density of the unburnt charge (kg/m³); A<sub>f</sub> is the flame front area (m²); S<sub>b</sub> is the burning velocity of the front relative to the unburnt gas (m/s). In a naturally aspirated engine ρ<sub>u</sub> is about 6 kg/m³ at the spark and rises to about 12 to 13 kg/m³ during the main burn, because the charge is compressed.

The flame front area starts near zero at the plug, grows as the kernel becomes a large front, and shrinks again when the front reaches the piston, the head and the far wall. So the burning rate is small at first, peaks in the middle of the burn and tails off at the end: the S-shaped mass fraction burned curve.
This is why chamber shape and plug position matter. A compact chamber with a central plug gives a short flame path and a large front for most of the burn (see combustion chambers).

The rate of pressure rise is the slope of the p–θ curve, dp/dθ, in bar per degree of crank angle (bar/°CA). Between two measured points the average is (p2 − p1) ÷ (θ2 − θ1). The first law of thermodynamics for the gas in the cylinder links it to the heat released:

Two things follow. The same heat released into a larger volume raises the pressure less, so a burn that happens late, when the piston is far down, gives a gentle slope. And a fast burn near TDC gives a steep slope and a high, early peak. A smooth petrol engine peaks at about 1 to 3 bar/°CA; much steeper slopes make the engine rough and noisy and load the bearings.

The figure compares three burn lengths in one engine. The fast burn gives the highest, earliest peak and the most work, but the roughest running; the slow burn peaks low and late and wastes heat to the exhaust. Good design aims at a burn that is fast but not violent.

items: Turbulence: the strongest effect. More turbulence wrinkles the front and raises ST; squish and tumble supply it (see air motion).
Fuel–air ratio: fastest slightly rich of stoichiometric; very lean or very rich mixtures burn slowly.
Temperature and pressure: a hotter charge burns faster; a higher compression ratio raises both and so raises flame speed.
Residual gas and EGR: burnt gas left in or fed back dilutes the charge and slows the flame.
Engine speed: flame speed rises almost in proportion to speed through turbulence, so the burn takes about the same crank degrees.
Engine size: a larger bore means a longer flame path, so the burn takes more time and more degrees at the same speed.

examples.question: The normal trace in the figure reads 24.9 bar at TDC and 45.4 bar at 10° aTDC. The engine runs at 3000 rev/min. (a) Find the average rate of pressure rise between the two points in bar/°CA. (b) Convert it to bar/ms. (c) The steepest slope of the same trace is 2.3 bar/°CA. Why is the average lower?
steps: At 3000 rev/min the crank turns 0.006 × 3000 = 18° each millisecond.
The average over 10° includes the gentler parts of the curve on either side of the steepest point, which lies near 5° aTDC, so it is below the 2.3 bar/°CA peak.
examples.answer: (a) 2.05 bar/°CA. (b) 36.9 bar/ms. (c) An average over an interval is always at or below the steepest slope inside it.

examples.question: In the same engine (clearance volume 62.4 cm³, a flat disc 10.75 mm deep at TDC) the flame near TDC is a cylinder of radius 35 mm spanning the full depth. The unburnt charge has density 12 kg/m³ and the front burns into it at 6 m/s. The mixture is stoichiometric (air–fuel ratio 14.7, so fuel is 1/15.7 of the charge) and the fuel releases 44 MJ/kg. Estimate the mass burning rate, the heat release per degree at 3000 rev/min, and dp/dθ (take γ = 1.35 and V ≈ clearance volume).
steps: Front area: A<sub>f</sub> = 2π r h = 2π × 0.035 × 0.01075 = 2.364 × 10⁻³ m².
Per degree: the crank turns 18 000 °/s, so 0.170 ÷ 18 000 = 9.46 × 10⁻⁶ kg = 9.46 mg of charge per degree.
Check: this lies within the 1 to 3 bar/°CA of a smooth engine.
examples.answer: About 0.170 kg/s of charge burns, releasing 26.5 J/°CA and raising the pressure by about 1.5 bar/°CA.

traps: Laminar burning velocity is below 1 m/s; quoting 20 m/s for S<sub>L</sub> is wrong. Tens of m/s is the flame travel velocity seen from the cylinder head.
High flame speed alone does not fix dp/dθ: the front area, the unburnt density and the cylinder volume at that moment all enter.
bar/°CA, bar/ms and bar/s are different units: 2.05 bar/°CA is 36.9 bar/ms at 3000 rev/min but 24.6 bar/ms at 2000 rev/min.
The slope between two points is an average; the steepest slope lies inside the interval and is higher.
A faster burn gives more work only up to a point: past it the engine becomes rough and the end gas, though it has less time, is squeezed harder.

quiz.q: Define flame travel velocity and give its unit.
quiz.a: The distance the flame front moves across the chamber divided by the time taken, measured relative to the cylinder head; m/s.

quiz.q: Write the mass burning rate in terms of the flame front.
quiz.a: ṁ<sub>b</sub> = ρ<sub>u</sub> A<sub>f</sub> S<sub>b</sub>: unburnt density × flame front area × burning velocity.

quiz.q: Why is the turbulent burning velocity larger than the laminar one?
quiz.a: Turbulence wrinkles and folds the front, raising its area, so more fresh charge meets the reaction zone each second; S<sub>T</sub> ≈ S<sub>L</sub> + u′.

quiz.q: Why does the same heat release give a smaller pressure rise late in expansion?
quiz.a: dp/dθ ≈ (γ − 1)(dQ/dθ)/V near the burn, and V is larger late in expansion, while the falling piston also lowers the pressure.

quiz.q: Pressure is 25 bar at 8° aTDC and 55 bar at 22° aTDC. Find the average rate of pressure rise.
An engine at 2000 rev/min shows 2 bar/°CA. Express this in bar/ms.
Compare the fast (25°) and slow (50°) burns in the figure on work, smoothness and exhaust temperature.
quiz.a: Fast: peak 59.8 bar at 10.5° aTDC, 3.8 bar/°CA, most work (9.57 bar) but rough. Slow: peak 37.8 bar at 21.9° aTDC, 1.0 bar/°CA, least work (8.97 bar) and hotter exhaust because heat is released late.

beyond: Development engines record cylinder pressure every 0.1° with piezoelectric sensors and turn it into a heat release curve with the first-law equation above. Flame speed correlations for each fuel feed three-dimensional CFD models that predict the burn before metal is cut. Search for heat release analysis, turbulent flame speed correlation and Damköhler number.

figure.caption: The same engine with three burn lengths, all starting at 10° bTDC: a shorter burn gives a higher, earlier peak and a steeper rise. The dashed chord on the normal trace is the worked example’s average slope, 2.05 bar per degree.

spec.aria: Three computed pressure traces. A 25 degree burn peaks at 59.8 bar at 10.5 degrees after TDC, steepest slope 3.8 bar per degree. A 35 degree burn peaks at 50.3 bar at 15.6 degrees, 2.3 bar per degree. A 50 degree burn peaks at 37.8 bar at 21.9 degrees, 1.0 bar per degree. A chord joins 24.9 bar at TDC and 45.4 bar at 10 degrees on the normal trace.
